sections.title: Climb the ladder
sections.intro: The `web` pods can't reach the `cart` Service. Everyone has a theory. Test one layer at a time, from the bottom up — the first rung that fails is your answer.

questions.prompt: Before testing any networking, what do you confirm, and why?
options: That the pods are Running *and* Ready
That no NetworkPolicy exists in the namespace
That CoreDNS is running in kube-system
That kube-proxy is running on every node
questions.explanation: If the pods aren't Ready, every rung above them fails for a reason that has nothing to do with the network. Checking first keeps you from debugging the wrong layer.

questions.prompt: The pods are Ready. Why test in the order Pod IP → ClusterIP → DNS name, rather than just curling the Service name?
options: It matches the order in the Service spec
Each layer sits on the one below it
The Service-name test is unreliable
DNS is the slowest test, so it goes last
questions.explanation: Curling the name alone tells you *something* is broken somewhere in three layers. The ladder tells you which one.

questions.prompt: Rung 1: from a `web` pod, you curl a `cart` pod's IP directly. What do you conclude?
questions.snippet:
$ kubectl exec web-1 -- curl -m 3 10.244.2.17:8080
curl: (7) Failed to connect to 10.244.2.17 port 8080: Connection refused
options: kube-proxy is down on that node
The packet arrived — nothing listens on that port
A NetworkPolicy is rejecting the traffic
The CNI is broken between these pods
questions.explanation: Refused vs. timed out is the most valuable split on this rung. A timeout means packets aren't arriving (CNI or policy). A refusal means they arrived and nothing was listening there. You can check what the app listens on with `ss -ltn` inside the pod, if the image has it.

questions.prompt: The app was actually listening on 3000. You retry on the right port and rung 1 passes. Now rung 2: curl the Service's ClusterIP. A teammate says "just ping the ClusterIP first, it's quicker." Why not?
options: ClusterIPs block ICMP as a security default
Ping is too slow to be a useful signal
Ping needs root inside the container
ClusterIPs only answer on Service ports, not ICMP
questions.explanation: A failed ping to a ClusterIP is meaningless, and it's a classic way to send everyone down the wrong path. Test with `curl` or `nc` on the Service port.

questions.prompt: Curl to the ClusterIP times out. Before you suspect kube-proxy itself, what's the cheapest, most likely check?
options: Check CoreDNS logs
Dump iptables on the node
`kubectl get endpoints cart`
Restart kube-proxy on every node
questions.explanation: A wrong selector is far more common than a broken kube-proxy, and checking it is one read-only command. Rule out configuration before you rule out a component.

questions.prompt: Endpoints come back empty. Compare these. What's wrong?
questions.snippet:
$ kubectl get svc cart -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}'
{"app":"cart-svc"}

$ kubectl get pods -l app=cart --show-labels
cart-5d-abc   1/1   Running   app=cart,pod-template-hash=5d
options: The pods aren't Ready, so they're excluded
The CNI never assigned the pods IPs
kube-proxy is down on the pods' node
The selector says `cart-svc`; the pods say `cart`
questions.explanation: That's a config issue that looks exactly like a component failure. Fix the selector, and endpoints show up within seconds. Note also that Endpoints only list *Ready* pods, so not-Ready pods produce the same `<none>`.

questions.prompt: Selector fixed, endpoints populated, but the ClusterIP curl now returns "connection refused." What's left at this rung?
options: kube-proxy's rules are stale
DNS is resolving to an old ClusterIP
`targetPort` doesn't match the container's port
The CNI overlay is dropping return traffic
questions.explanation: Traffic is reaching the pod, but on a port nobody listens to. That's the same refused-vs-timeout reasoning as rung 1, one layer up.

questions.prompt: Rung 2 passes after fixing `targetPort`. Rung 3: the name fails. What does that isolate it to, and what's a good control test?
questions.snippet:
$ kubectl exec web-1 -- nslookup cart.shop.svc.cluster.local
;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached
options: The CNI — DNS packets are being dropped
DNS only — test `nslookup kubernetes.default`
kube-proxy — the name maps to a ClusterIP
The app — it isn't registered with DNS
questions.explanation: Every layer below DNS is proven to work, so this is entirely name resolution. `kubernetes.default` always exists, which makes it a clean control.

questions.prompt: Final sanity check: `web` is in namespace `storefront`, `cart` is in `shop`, and the app code calls `http://cart:3000`. Is DNS broken?
options: No — short names only resolve in the same namespace
Yes — CoreDNS should find it anywhere
No — a NetworkPolicy is blocking it
Yes — restart CoreDNS to refresh records
questions.explanation: This is one of the most common reasons DNS looks broken when it isn't. The resolver tries `cart.storefront.svc.cluster.local`, which doesn't exist.

sections.title: Read the signal
sections.intro: Each one stands alone. Which rung, which component, and why?

questions.prompt: Which component is most likely broken?
questions.snippet:
$ kubectl exec pod-a -- curl -m 3 10.244.1.9:8080   # same node
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
$ kubectl exec pod-a -- curl -m 3 10.244.3.4:8080   # different node
curl: (28) Connection timed out
options: The app running on 10.244.3.4
CoreDNS on the second node
The CNI's cross-node overlay or routing
kube-proxy on the second node
questions.explanation: Comparing same-node and cross-node results is what separates "CNI is down" from "the overlay between nodes is broken." Often this ends up with the infra team.

questions.prompt: Only `web` → `payments` traffic times out. Every other pod pair works. What's the first suspect?
options: The payments image listening on the wrong port
A crashed CNI plugin on payments' node
A NetworkPolicy — selective blocking is by design
kube-proxy failing for that one Service
questions.explanation: A broken network fails indiscriminately, while a policy fails selectively. Fix the policy's *intent* instead of deleting it. And note that policies only take effect if your CNI enforces them (Flannel alone doesn't).

questions.prompt: Pod-to-pod works and Endpoints are populated, but ClusterIP traffic times out from pods on one node only. What do you check on that node?
options: kube-proxy on that node — its pod and its rules
CoreDNS — that node can't resolve the name
The Service selector — it skips that node
The app's port — it differs on that node
questions.explanation: Failing on one node only means something local to that node. kube-proxy runs per node, so a crashed or stale instance breaks only the Services on that node.

questions.prompt: Your cluster runs Cilium with kube-proxy replacement. A teammate can't find any kube-proxy pods or iptables rules for Services. Is that the bug?
options: Yes — Services always need iptables rules
No — it's a DNS problem instead
No — Cilium handles Services in eBPF there
Yes — reinstall kube-proxy on every node
questions.explanation: Know which data plane you're actually running. Looking for kube-proxy in a kube-proxy-free cluster is debugging something that isn't there.

questions.prompt: One pod can't resolve any cluster names. Every other pod can. Its resolv.conf looks like this. What's wrong?
questions.snippet:
$ kubectl exec metrics-agent -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
nameserver 10.0.0.2
search ec2.internal
options: It's using the node's resolver, not cluster DNS
The kube-dns Service has no endpoints
The CNI didn't give it a DNS address
CoreDNS is down for this one pod
questions.explanation: A single pod failing points at its own config, not the cluster's DNS. A healthy cluster pod has the kube-dns ClusterIP as its nameserver and `svc.cluster.local` search domains.

questions.prompt: CoreDNS pods are all Running and Ready, but no pod can resolve anything, and this started right after an upgrade. What do you check?
questions.snippet:
$ kubectl get endpoints -n kube-system kube-dns
NAME       ENDPOINTS
kube-dns   <none>
options: The CNI on the CoreDNS pods' nodes
The kube-dns selector vs. the CoreDNS pod labels
Restart CoreDNS so it re-registers
Every pod's resolv.conf, one by one
questions.explanation: This is the same failure as a mismatched app selector, just one layer up. Healthy pods behind a Service that selects nothing look exactly like dead pods.

questions.prompt: Every in-cluster test passes: pod IP, ClusterIP, DNS name. External users still can't reach the site. Where now?
options: Back down to the CNI — retest pod IPs
CoreDNS — external names resolve there
kube-proxy — external traffic uses it first
The edge — the Ingress controller or cloud LB
questions.explanation: The ladder passing is a result too: it proves the cluster's internal networking works. Don't go back down a ladder you just climbed.
